problem: Given that $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\theta =\theta (t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=\sqrt{2}$ at the point where $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ find $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$

feedback.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }\,(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{3}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3},$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot [-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})] \\ \frac{1}{3} & =\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}\cdot (-2) \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
